eb-ask: The 5 A's: ask, acquire, appraise, apply, assess, always in that order.
PICO(T): patient or problem, intervention, comparison, outcome, time; only foreground (comparison) questions fit PICO.
Search TRIP first, then PubMed Clinical Queries, then the Cochrane Library.
Starts with the disease and looks back = case-control (odds ratio); starts with the exposure and follows forward = cohort (incidence, relative risk).
Case-control suits rare diseases; cohort suits rare exposures.
Cross-sectional = one snapshot, prevalence; ecological = group averages, prone to the ecological fallacy.
The RCT is the only true experiment and the best single study for a therapy question.
Pyramid, bottom to top: lab and animal → case reports and expert opinion → ecological → cross-sectional → case-control → cohort → RCT → systematic review and meta-analysis → guideline.
Meta-analysis = systematic review + pooled summary statistic; a literature review has no method.
GRADE rates the certainty of evidence (high to very low); AGREE appraises guidelines; CONSORT reports RCTs, STROBE observational studies.
Efficacy = ideal conditions (academic RCT); effectiveness = everyday practice.
Knowledge gap → efficacy and effectiveness studies; knowing gap → dissemination; knowing-to-doing gap → implementation.
eb-appraise: Internal validity = believable for the subjects; external validity = applies to your patients.
Bias = systematic error; confounding = a third factor tied to exposure and outcome; chance = random sampling variation.
Randomization balances known and unknown confounders; blinding prevents measurement bias.
Intention-to-treat = analyze everyone as randomized; per-protocol = only those who completed.
Precision = repeatable; accuracy = true. Standardization = same rules; calibration = scores agree.
Incidence = new cases over time (cohort); prevalence = existing cases now (cross-sectional).
Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN), SnNout, for screening; specificity = TN/(TN+FP), SpPin, for confirming.
As prevalence falls, PPV falls and NPV rises; sensitivity and specificity don't change.
A ratio of 1 = no difference, above 1 = harmful, below 1 = protective; a CI that includes 1 = not significant.
NNT = 1/ARR, rounded up; lower is better.
Type I = false positive (alpha, 0.05); type II = false negative (beta); power = 1 − beta.
The median beats the mean for skewed data; statistical significance isn't clinical importance.
